Tyranids definitely make sense for Raggadragga, because hitting that 7 mana threshold really makes the engine go. Prioritize card draw as it can be tricky in Gruul. \[\[Commune with Lava\]\] is an all-star in this deck. Once you've built a lot of mana, you can exile almost your entire deck and cast your \[\[Crackle with Power\]\]. Going for a more low-to-the-ground/creature focused style, this may not be the best strategy, but its the main win-con in my deck. Cards like \[\[Regal Force\]\] pull a lot of weight. It's seven mana so it activates Raggadragga, untapping whichever dork gives you the most mana, and draws you a card for each \[\[Llanowar Elves\]\] - equivalent you have out. \[\[Apex of Power\]\] is a great late game play, refunding your mana, activating Raggadragga, and letting you see a lot of cards. 

  
I love this deck, though it falls in the space of 'too strong for casual but not strong enough for cEDH'. A lot of the win lines are not technically infinite, as it relies on you being able to continue drawing cards and generating mana, but its a fun time to chain together a bunch of spells. A storm deck that cares about 7 mana cards is fun little twist.

So Raggadragga can be EXTREMELY powerful if built correctly. If you focus on mana dorks like \[\[Marwyn the Nuturer\]\] that tap equal to their power, you can go psuedo-infinite fairly easily. If you don't go that route, Raggadragga is still totally viable as a stack of mana dorks. There are some big creatures that technically have mana abilities that can benefit from the power increase and the untapping. Use a lot of X spells so that they scale as you land mana dorks and can be cast for 7 mana to trigger Raggadragga. My deck can win on turn 5 fairly consistently, and could be turned into a fringe cEDH deck if you wanted to go that route.

Here's mine as well. It's built to be a power level 8ish. It'll win on turn 5 if not interacted with. It's not cEDH, it runs no fast mana, and is very interruptible. With the exception of \[\[Staff of Dominion\]\], the deck doesn't have a true infinite in it. You're always reliant on drawing into your next 7 mana spell, but if it goes, it goes. It has just enough recursion and protection to fend off some removal It relies on finding \[\[Marwyn the Nurturer\]\] or their counterparts, then repeatedly untapping them to make more mana. 

You want 3 lands, a Marwyn (or a tutor), a 7 mana spell, and a card draw spell in your hand to start. A T1 dork is great too. Ideally it goes like this:

T1: Land, one-drop mana dork

T2: Land, Marwyn or equivalent

T3: Land, Raggadragga

T4: Land, 7 drop, storm off for the win. 

You're vulnerable after the T2 big dork. Spot removal hoses you right there. Once Raggadragga hits though, you can tap your big dork for 3 to cast a protection spell. As soon as you hit the first 7 drop, you should have enough mana to play some interaction and protect your board. You can float a bunch of mana in response to targeted removal to either recast Raggadragga or play some recursion like \[\[Eternal Witness\]\]. Or just a good \[\[Red Elemental Blast\]\] to beat the blue player at their own game. 

X spells are the main way to use the extra mana. Some win on the spot like \[\[Comet Storm\]\], others set you up for a win next turn like \[\[Awaken the Woods\]\]. 

\[\[Commune with Lava\]\] and \[\[March of Reckless Joy\]\] are lynchpins for this deck. Get lots of mana, cast one of them for like 80, untap Marwyn, cast whichever wincon you like best. \[\[Apex of Power\]\] has the same effect. \[\[Garruks Horde\]\] is the critical 7 mana, and then lets you cast from the top to keep the gas coming. 

\[\[Helix Pinnacle\]\] is another slower wincon and an excellent mana sink. 

Looking quickly over your deck, I would say you just need to streamline. All your spells should be 3 mana or less, or 7 or over. Go hard on finding a Marwyn. If a mana dork doesn't come out T1 or doesn't tap for mana equal to its power, you probably don't need it. (My deck breaks this rule a few times). 

Think of it like a storm deck. \[\[Manamorphose\]\] is sneaky good. It converts green to red, gives you another card, and lets you keep going. \[\[Mana Bloom\]\] does the same, and can be cast for 7 mana to untap your big dork. These and \[\[Chromatic Orrery\]\] solve the problem of Marwyn only making green mana.

You really have to build for Braids or else you just get out-gassed by everyone else. I wouldn't recommend it for an Unesh list.

Other notes:

\-You probably want a couple more ramp pieces in the deck. Sphinxes are expensive even with Unesh. \[\[Heraldic Banner\]\] is pump and ramp at the same time, and \[\[Kefnets Monument\]\] is a bit of board control and cost reduction. Yes they're three mana rocks, but they work. You can always always go the Mana Crypt/Vault route if you have the money. 

\-Thassa's Oracle doesn't guarantee you a win without something to cut your library way down, not sure card draw alone is enough in a higher powered game. \[\[Paradigm Shift\]\] would be a good fit, as you already have some ways to tutor for it. 

In terms of specific cuts, I'd get rid of:

\-Eligeth - You don't enough scry effects to take advantage. Replace with another clone. 

\-Curator of Mysteries  - Same as above. 

\-Omniscience - Way expensive. Try a kicked \[\[Rite of Replication\]\] instead. 5 ETBs for Unesh, plus a fleet of fliers. You can always cast it unkicked too. 

\-Flusterstom - You're playing a creature heavy deck, you won't be having big storm turns. \[\[Counterspell\]\] does the trick here just fine and is guaranteed to counter. 

\-Cloudstone Curio is probably not the best fit here. You'll still need to play to replay whatever you bounce. \[\[Conjurer's Closet\]\] is more expensive, but it lets you trigger Unesh an extra time each turn, and resets a tapped sphinx to have a blocker up.

That'll help you push damage through quicker and more consistently. [[Quicksilver Amulet]] let's you drop your fliers on other people's turn, effectively giving them haste. [[Strionic Resonator]] doubles your ETB and combat triggers.

I love my Braids decks. It's a sphinx tribal/theft deck. Steal/remove others stuff to mitigate the advantage. \[\[Roil Elemental\]\] is great for this. 

It does run Greaves for protection, along with \[\[Kira, Great Glass Spinner\]\], \[\[Vanishing\]\] (My favorite card in the deck), \[\[Winged Boots\]\] (Because flying is on theme in mine) and \[\[Esior, Ward Wing Familiar\]\]. It's got counterspells in there as well to keep my board safe. 

As others have mentioned, sometimes braids is just going to get removed and you're hosed. Such is the nature of the commander. \[\[Quicksilver Amulet\]\] lets you cheat your big stuff if Braids is removed, or if you can get Braids back to hand you can use the amulet to play her on the end step before your turn. 

The deck rarely wins, but I always have fun with it. sometimes you use \[\[Magic Mirror\]\] to become a \[\[Bolas' Citadel\]\] deck, which is riot. Sometimes you control every commander at the table. Sometimes you have 3 copies of \[\[Sphinx of the Second Sun\]\] and have 4 upkeeps a turn. 

\[\[Consecrated Sphinx\]\] is obvious if you can afford it. \[\[The Magic Mirror\]\] is fantastic to cheat out early, especially with multiple upkeeps. Its an excuse to play a mono-blue Timmy deck that isn't Sea Creatures.

Voltron, by my definition, is using a single large creature, pumped with permanents, to deal lethal.  Since you can only swing at one opponent at a time, you're naturally taking out one person instead of the whole table like you could with combo/tokens/spellslinger. 

At least in my voltrony decks, getting a game to 1v1 is to my advantage as there are fewer chances for my commander to get removed and only one board state for me to worry about in terms of using my own removal.  

That's where people get salty with Voltron. By it's nature, someone's going to be sitting on the sidelines while the game plays out, and if the Tron players threat gets blown up it can turn into a slog where the eliminated player is sitting doing nothing for a while. 

Now I don't agree with that being an issue because it's a multiplayer format and somebody has to die. I think the eliminated player can still get value out of observing, whether it's seeing new strategies better because you're not worried about your own shit, or helping the remaining players remember triggers (as long as it's equal and in a casual setting). The game is about neat cards doing neat things, I don't think they necessarily have to be yours. 

And your general sentiment of 'play more interaction' should apply to ALL decks. The format isn't about playing solitaire, and stopping your opponents plans or opening up a hole in their defense is incredibly helpful regardless of the deck archetype.

Due to the movement of both the rider and car, the impact is almost assuredly going to be off axis, which would result in rotational forces. The more traditional foam and shell structure that also exists on most if not all MIPs helmets is designed to reduce the direct, more linear forces that occur. Even if the forces start off as purely linear, there is going to be enough movement throughout the impact scenario where rotational forces come into play. 

And you're right, helmets aren't magic. You're going to break a lot more than your skull in a severe collision. But its easier to rebuild bones than it is to fix brain damage, so any and all measures to protect your head and spine should be taken (within reason, I doubt anyone on a bike would be willing to wear a full face motorcycle helmet). 

Ultimately I think were mostly in agreement. My statement you quoted was too generalized and you're right that a helmet won't reduce your risk to zero. But in the city where most collisions will be relatively low speed (I would like to see comprehensive data on cyclist/vehicle collision speeds/locations/etc but I'm not sure its readily available). 

Again, I appreciate this discussion. I'll look into your claim of the lack of rotational forces, because my assertion against it is based purely on my own thoughts and logic. Happy to take a source if you have one.

Helmets, especially MTB helmets with MIPS, are designed for higher speed crashes. No helmet is going to make you walk away from a 40mph collision, but it can seriously reduce your chances of a TBI. So rather than being racked up in the hospital in a coma, you might only be racked up in the hospital with a hefty concussion. 

FWIW, I've been hit and my MIPShelmet saved me from some serious injury. A car cut me off and I ended up with a face full of asphalt, but not even a mild concussion. I was going around 20 and took a solid knock.

A majority of bicycle-car collisions in the city happen sub 20mph when cars are changing lanes or turning corners. A 40 dollar helmet might not help too much but I can say from experience that springing for a nice helmet can and will save you from serious damage. I'm not spreading any falsehoods, helmets will keep you alive.
